summary: Sohail Shaikh and Ankush Rastogi introduce the '100-tool agent trap,' where a fat agent architecture loads every tool definition into the system prompt on every request. This works acceptably with 10 tools but degrades as the catalog grows: the model calls wrong functions, confuses similar tools, invents tool names, and responds more slowly. At 741 tools, tool descriptions alone consume approximately 127,000 tokens before the user query is even considered. Accuracy drops from 78% at 10 tools to 13.6% at 741 tools, while time-to-first-token latency grows significantly. The proposed solution is the Semantic Tool Router, analogous to RAG for tools. Tool descriptions are embedded offline and stored in a vector database. At runtime, the user query is embedded, nearest-neighbor search retrieves the top K tools (K=5 recommended), and only those schemas are injected into the model call. This keeps context small, latency stable, and accuracy above 83% across catalog sizes. The code implementation is straightforward: loop through the tool catalog, embed each description, store vectors with tool name and details; at runtime embed the query, compare via cosine similarity, retrieve top tools, and call the model only with routed schemas. A live example with a 200-tool agent demonstrates that the router not only adds the right tool but removes wrong tools from the model's choice set. A six-step production checklist covers locking tools in one place (name, description, schema, owner, version), building the index, writing the router, wiring it into the agent loop, evaluating at K=3, 5, and 10, and monitoring production with logging and re-embedding on changes. Community validation includes Anthropic's MCP on-demand tool loading (150k to 2k tokens), open-source projects like Aurelio Labs' semantic router and MCP Zero, and benchmarks like Toolbench and Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard. Trade-offs include router misses (handled by widening K or fallback passes), weak tool descriptions requiring user-language intent and entities, and rare tools needing description rewrites. The presenters stress this is a focused sprint, not a platform rewrite, and caution against over-engineering small systems with 10-15 tools where static loading is fine.

sections.title: Speaker Introductions
sections.summary: Sohail Shaikh introduces himself as a data scientist at Prosodica with a background in AI, NLP, analytics, and engineering. Ankush Rastogi introduces himself as a senior data solutions engineer at Prosodica with over a decade in AI, data engineering, and production systems.

sections.title: The Fat Agent Problem
sections.summary: The simplest approach loads every tool definition on every request, creating a 'fat agent.' This works with ~10 tools but as the catalog grows the model calls wrong functions, confuses similar tools, invents tool names, and responds slowly. At 741 tools, schemas consume ~127,000 tokens before the user query is considered.

sections.title: Accuracy, Latency, and Cost Breakdown
sections.summary: Fat agent accuracy drops from 78% at 10 tools to 40% at ~100 tools to 13.6% at 741 tools, while semantic router stays above 83%. The lost-in-the-middle problem causes the model to ignore mid-context tools. At 100k requests/day, billions of tokens are spent describing tools. Just-in-time routing reduces tool context by ~99%. At 500 tools, fat agent first-token latency can exceed 5 seconds.

sections.title: Fat Agent vs Semantic Router Comparison
sections.summary: Side-by-side comparison: fat agent loads all schemas every request, growing the prompt. Semantic router retrieves 3-5 relevant tools per query, keeping context small. Below 20 tools a router is unnecessary; above 50 it is justified.

sections.title: How Semantic Routing Works
sections.summary: Semantic routing is analogous to RAG for tools. Each tool description is embedded and stored in a vector index offline. At runtime, the user query is embedded with the same model, nearest-neighbor search returns the top K tools, and only those schemas are injected into the model call.

sections.title: Just-in-Time Context Injection and Evaluation Methodology
sections.summary: Just-in-time context injection applies lazy-loading to LLM context. Anthropic's MCP achieved 98.7% token reduction. Evaluation measures tool selection accuracy, time-to-first-token, input tokens, and cost per thousand calls. K was swept at 3, 5, and 10, with K=5 as recommended default.

sections.title: Benchmark Results and Implementation Patterns
sections.summary: Benchmark results confirm fat agent accuracy drops sharply while router stays above 83%. Implementation has three steps: offline catalog building and embedding, runtime query embedding and nearest-neighbor search returning top K tools, and fetching only selected schemas for the model call with logging.

sections.title: Code Walkthrough
sections.summary: Sohail walks through the code: loop through the tool catalog, embed each description, store vectors in a vector database with tool name and details. At runtime, embed the user query, compare via cosine similarity, retrieve top relevant tools, and call the model only with routed schemas. Works with any embedding model and vector database; reuses existing RAG infrastructure.

sections.title: Semantic Routing in Action
sections.summary: A 200-tool agent example: a flight query returns search_flights, book_flight, calendar_check; a weather query returns get_weather, get_forecast. The router not only adds the right tool but removes wrong tools from the model's choice set, preventing cross-tool confusion.

sections.title: Production Implementation Checklist
sections.summary: Six-step checklist: (1) Lock tools in one place with name, description, schema, owner, version. (2) Build the index by embedding each description. (3) Write the router: embed query, search index, take top K, fetch schema. (4) Wire it into the agent loop so the tool list comes from the router, not a hard-coded catalog. (5) Evaluate at K=3, 5, and 10, picking the smallest K meeting accuracy targets. (6) Monitor production: log selected tools, final calls, failures, fallbacks, and re-embed when descriptions change. This is a focused sprint, not a platform rewrite.

sections.title: Community Validation and Open-Source Resources
sections.summary: Anthropic published on-demand tool loading with MCP, reporting 150k to 2k token reduction. Developers have raised similar issues in mainstream agent and SDK projects. Open-source projects like MCP Zero explore routing at thousands of tools. Aurelio Labs offers an open-source semantic router. Toolbench and Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard are useful benchmarks. The ecosystem already exists; no need to invent from scratch.

sections.title: Trade-offs and Risks
sections.summary: Four trade-offs: (1) Router miss—handle by widening K, second retrieval pass, or broader tool group. (2) Weak tool descriptions—write in user language with intent, action, and key entities. (3) Rare tools—monitor data misses and rewrite descriptions. (4) Over-engineering small systems—static loading is fine for 10-15 tools; routing pays off when prompt size, latency, or confusion becomes a real production problem.

sections.title: Conclusion and Key Takeaways
sections.summary: Final takeaways: tool overload hurts accuracy; tokens are both cost and latency; semantic routing is RAG for tools—index descriptions, retrieve at runtime, inject only what is needed. Start simple with K=5, log every decision, evaluate against real test sets, and improve tool descriptions over time. The goal is to stop forcing models to reason over irrelevant tools. References include semantic routing libraries, Toolbench, Berkeley leaderboard, Anthropic MCP write-up, and vector stores like Pinecone and Qdrant.
